h1: Testing a brewpub idea with pop up nights before you commit
title: Test a Brewpub Idea With Pop-Up Nights | Craft Beer School
desc: How to test a brewpub concept with pop-up nights before signing a lease: what to run, what to measure, a break-even sum and the licensing limits.
teaser: A lease and a brewhouse are expensive ways to find out nobody wants your menu. A few pop-up nights are cheap ways to find out first.
standfirst: Before you commit to a brewpub, you can test the concept with small events at a licensed partner venue. The point is to measure demand, not to enjoy the evening. Here is what to run, what to count and where the licensing limits sit.
sections: What a pop-up can and cannot prove

A pop-up can tell you whether people will come, what they will order and what they will pay. It cannot tell you whether your kitchen copes at 200 covers, whether your brewhouse hits yield or whether the lease is affordable on a quiet Tuesday. Be honest about that from the start. A pop-up de-risks demand and price. Everything else needs a model.

Write down the question each night answers before you hold it. A night with no question becomes a party.

Alcohol is a state subject in India. Selling or serving beer without the right permission can end the whole project before it starts. You cannot simply set up a stall and pour. Rules and fees differ by state and change, so ask a licensing consultant or your state excise department what an event or a partnership needs.

The practical routes are usually these:

  • Hold the night at a venue that already has a licence to serve, with their consent and their licence covering the sale.
  • Work with a licensed brewery or contract brewer for the beer, instead of making it yourself.
  • Run the first tests with food, non-alcoholic drinks and tasting-style conversations while the paperwork is pending.

Do not guess. This is process guidance, not legal advice. Our guide to takeaway beer rules in India shows how much the detail varies.

One night tells you very little. Three tell you about repeat interest. A simple plan:

  1. A launch night with your full draft menu and food, at your target price.
  2. A second night two weeks later with the same menu, to see who returns.
  3. A third night with one change, such as a lower price or a different food pairing, to test sensitivity.

Use the same venue each time if you can. Changing venue changes the crowd and muddies the results. Keep a guest list and a sign-up sheet for email or phone numbers. Names that appear on both nights are your best early signal of loyalty.

Pick five numbers and write them down on the night:

  • Guests who came, split by booking and walk-in.
  • Average spend per guest on drinks and on food.
  • Which beers and dishes sold out and which barely moved.
  • Guests who returned for the second night.
  • Sign-ups for the next event.

Ask two simple questions on a card. What would make you come every week? What put you off? Short, honest answers beat a long survey. Our guide to forecasting beer volumes for a new brewpub shows how to turn these into a volume plan.
A break-even sum on round numbers

This is an illustration with made-up round numbers. Use your own. Say a brewpub has fixed costs of ₹5,00,000 a month: rent, salaries, utilities and loan repayments. Say average spend per guest is ₹900 and the cost of beer, food and consumables takes 30% of that. The contribution is ₹630 per guest.

Break-even guests per month = 5,00,000 / 630 = about 794. Over 30 days that is roughly 26 guests a day, on average, before you earn a rupee of profit. If your pop-up nights drew 60 guests with a ₹900 spend but only 10 came back, the lease needs more than a good launch night.

The model is simple on purpose. Its job is to turn a feeling into a threshold you can compare with real counts.
Set pass and fail before the first night

Decide your threshold on paper before you hold the event. For example: at least a third of launch guests return for the second night, average spend within 10% of your plan and at least two beers that guests rate above average on the card. If you miss two of three, change the concept and test again before signing anything.

The temptation after a good evening is to read it as proof. Friends, family and curious locals inflate every first night. The second night, with fewer friends and more strangers, is the one to trust.
Where the numbers meet the business plan

The counts feed a plan that covers the whole business: capacity, staffing, pricing, cash flow and payback. A pop-up gives you inputs. It does not give you the structure that turns those inputs into a decision on a lease, a loan or an equity round. That structure is the part of costing and planning that is hard to learn from a template.
faqs: Can I sell beer at a pop-up in India?
Only with the right permission, which is a state matter and changes. Hold the event at a licensed venue or with a licensed partner. Ask a licensing consultant what the arrangement needs.
How many pop-up nights are enough?
Three is a sensible minimum. One shows launch interest, a second shows repeat interest and a third tests a change in price or menu.
What is the most useful number from a pop-up?
The share of guests who return for the second night. It is harder to inflate than a launch night crowd.
